title: A Weak US Jobs Report Just Took a Fed Rate Hike Off the Table — and India's Markets Are Surging on the News
excerpt: Nonfarm payrolls came in at just 57,000 against expectations of 115,000, sending the dollar to its biggest one-day drop in two months and pushing Indian equities back above the $5 trillion mark for the first time since the Iran crisis began.
body:
The most closely watched number in global finance just came in at less than half of what Wall Street expected — and for Indian investors, the implications could not be more welcome.

The United States added only 57,000 nonfarm payroll jobs in June, roughly half the 115,000 economists had forecast, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on Thursday. Payrolls for the previous two months were revised down by a combined 74,000, with May's gains dropping from 172,000 to 129,000. The unemployment rate fell to 4.2 per cent, but largely because the labour force participation rate slipped to 61.5 per cent — its lowest since March 2021 — rather than because of robust hiring.

The message was immediate and unambiguous: the Federal Reserve is now far less likely to raise interest rates this month.

## Markets React

Traders of short-term interest-rate futures priced in less than a 20 per cent chance of a July rate hike, down from roughly one in three before the report, according to CME Group. Even the odds of a September hike — which Fed Chair Kevin Warsh had signalled as likely after his hawkish debut at the June meeting — fell to around 60 per cent from 75 per cent.

The dollar index slid 0.52 per cent, its steepest single-day decline in two months, settling at 100.87. The euro climbed to $1.143 and the yen strengthened to 161 per dollar. Emerging-market currencies rallied broadly, gaining 0.3 per cent against the greenback.

"The slowdown in payroll growth challenges the narrative of renewed labour-market strength that has been building in recent months but, importantly, reinforces the view that the Federal Reserve is under little pressure to tighten policy," wrote Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management.

## India's Rally Extends

Indian equities, already on a four-session winning streak, surged on Friday as the weaker US data added fuel to a rally driven by falling oil prices and a rebound in the technology sector. The Sensex climbed as much as 655 points to cross the 78,150 mark, while the Nifty 50 rose over 200 points to trade above 24,370.

The IT index led the charge, gaining 3 per cent on Friday alone and extending gains for a second straight session. The rally reflects value-buying after a punishing 6.5 per cent drop in the prior four sessions and a deeper selloff earlier this year amid fears of AI disruption. With the weak US jobs report easing rate-hike anxiety, the sector — which earns the bulk of its revenue in dollars — found fresh tailwinds.

India's stock market has now regained the $5 trillion equity valuation milestone, marking a significant recovery from the depths of the Iran war-driven selloff. The BSE's total market capitalisation had slipped below $4.2 trillion in May as oil surged past $126 a barrel and foreign investors pulled $27 billion from Indian equities in the first half of the year.

Brent crude, now trading near $71 a barrel — down 43 per cent from its April war peak — has been the single biggest factor in India's turnaround. "The drop in oil prices is the single biggest factor for India, as it impacts growth, inflation, forex reserves, and fiscal deficit," said G. Chokkalingam, founder of Equinomics Research.

## Global Funds Are Coming Back

The macro improvement is not going unnoticed by global fund managers. A Reuters report this week revealed that daily selling by foreign funds has slowed markedly, while inflows into US-listed India-focused exchange-traded funds turned positive last week for the first time in more than a month.

"Two key headwinds have eased," said Todd McClone, a portfolio manager at William Blair Investment Management, which oversees about $65 billion. "India is among the most oversold markets we track. This macro improvement, alongside a more attractive valuation premium, strengthens the case to act."

Vikas Pershad, a portfolio manager at M&G, which manages roughly $450 billion, said his firm had "gradually reduced our India underweight" by doubling down on existing high-conviction holdings — capital freed up by scaling back positions in South Korea and Taiwan, where tech-heavy markets have undergone sharp corrections.

Average allocations to India among emerging-market funds had dropped below 10 per cent in April — the lowest since early 2021 — from a peak of 17.5 per cent in August 2024, according to Copley Fund Research. The tide now appears to be turning.

## The NRI Investor Takeaway

For NRI investors, the picture is shifting rapidly. A weaker US dollar improves rupee returns on Indian holdings, while lower rate-hike odds support both equity valuations and the Indian currency, which has recovered to around ₹94.50 per dollar from its May low of nearly ₹97.

The risk to watch is inflation. Average hourly earnings in the US still rose 3.5 per cent year-on-year in June, and Nick Timiraos of *The Wall Street Journal* noted that Fed policymakers view inflation — not employment — as the binding constraint. A strong CPI print in the coming weeks could reignite hike talk.

But for now, the confluence of falling oil, easing rate fears, and returning foreign capital has created the most favourable macro backdrop for Indian equities in months. India's outperformance over tech-heavy Asia — the Nifty gained 7 per cent from its June lows while the KOSPI crashed 8 per cent on Thursday — underscores a rotation that may have room to run.

**Sources:** Bureau of Labor Statistics; Reuters; CME FedWatch; The Hindu BusinessLine; The Indian Eye; Wall Street Journal
